351.title: Prescribed as for those before
351.hook: fasting prescribed so you may be mindful, and Allah wants ease for you (2:183–185)
351.howItsDone: Muslims fast from dawn to sunset through Ramadan; the sick and travelers may postpone days and make them up later, and those who cannot fast at all, such as the very old, feed a person in need for each day missed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, birr, and your line: righteousness is what you do. Did you keep the promise you found? Patience was the last thing on that list. Today, a whole month of it. Day three hundred fifty-one.

Imagine a rule that's strict on paper: no food, no water, from before dawn until sunset, for a whole month. Now read the fine print, and the fine print is generous. Sick? Don't fast; make it up later. Traveling? The same. Too old or frail to fast at all? Feed someone in need instead. Most rules get harder in the fine print. This one gets kinder. It's in al-Baqarah, in the same three verses that set the fast. Today: sawm.
screen: `STRICT ON PAPER.` → `THE FINE PRINT IS GENEROUS.` → `THREE VERSES THAT SET THE FAST.`

segments.voice: Last year you met the opening of this passage: fasting is prescribed for you, as it was prescribed for those before you, so that you may be mindful. That last word is taqwa, which you met two weeks ago on the first page of al-Baqarah. The fast is a school for it. Now read on. Verse one hundred eighty-four says: a set number of days. Whoever is sick or on a journey, an equal number of other days. And for those who can fast only with great hardship, a ransom: feeding a poor person. Then verse one hundred eighty-five names the month, Ramadan, the month the Qur'an was sent down, and repeats the exemption, and then gives the reason behind all of it. In Pickthall's words: “Allah desireth for you ease; He desireth not hardship for you.” The word for fasting is sawm, and at root it means to hold back, to abstain. The Qur'an uses the same word for Maryam's vow of silence: a sawm from speech. Bukhari keeps a scene from a journey in Ramadan. Some of the companions were fasting, some weren't, and Anas reports that neither group found fault with the other. Scholars across the schools teach that a traveler may choose, and that the sick should not harm themselves. The fast is demanding, and Muslims take it seriously. But the verse that commands it also guards the people keeping it. Mindfulness is the goal. Hardship isn't. Allah wants ease for you.
screen: `SO THAT YOU MAY BE MINDFUL` · `SICK OR TRAVELING: OTHER DAYS` · `SAWM: TO HOLD BACK` · `NEITHER GROUP FOUND FAULT`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: skip one snack mindfully. Only if it's safe for you; if you're unwell, pregnant, or have a condition that needs regular food, skip something else, like five minutes of scrolling. Sit now, and notice where in your day the snack usually lives. Picture the moment you'll reach for it. Picture not reaching. What does the small hunger feel like? What do you notice instead? Hold it lightly, without strain. The bell holds the time.
Sawm. Fasting; at root, holding back. Prescribed so you may be mindful, with ease written into it for the sick, the traveler and the frail. Today's word.
Your line: allah wants ease for you. Today, when you're hard on yourself or someone else, ask what the kind version of the rule would be. Day three hundred fifty-one.

original.note: Arabic: fasting, from a root meaning to hold back; also called siyam.

trapdoor: what you thought: a month of not eating.
what it means: a prescribed holding back, aimed at mindfulness, with ease built in for the sick, the traveler and the frail.
what a scholar hears: sawm means abstaining in general: 19:26 uses it for Maryam's vow of silence, and 2:185 grounds the exemptions in the principle that God wills ease.

352.title: Close enough to answer
352.hook: I am near, I answer the caller (2:186), set right inside the fasting verses
352.carry: near, in the middle of the fast
352.howItsDone: Many Muslims spend the last minutes before breaking the fast in personal supplication, following the hadith that the fasting person's du'a is not turned away, and the placement of 2:186 among the fasting verses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sawm, the fast, and your line: Allah wants ease for you. Where did you look for the kind version of a rule? Today, the verse that sits right in the middle of those fasting verses. Day three hundred fifty-two.

It's late afternoon in Ramadan. The fast has been long, the coffee headache came and went hours ago, and the kitchen smells of something that can't be eaten yet. Fifteen minutes to sunset. In some homes, this is when people go quiet. Someone sits with hands open. Someone else stirs the soup and whispers. Tradition counts this hour as a time when asking is heard. Part of the reason is a verse placed exactly here. Today: close enough to answer.
screen: `FIFTEEN MINUTES TO SUNSET.` → `HANDS OPEN, A WHISPER.` → `A VERSE PLACED EXACTLY HERE.`

segments.voice: Read the passage in order. Verse one hundred eighty-five: the month of Ramadan, ease not hardship. Verse one hundred eighty-seven: the nights of the fast, eating until the white thread of dawn shows against the black. And between them, verse one hundred eighty-six, which isn't about fasting at all. In Pickthall's words: “And when My servants question thee concerning Me, then surely I am nigh. I answer the prayer of the suppliant when he crieth unto Me.” Last year you heard how this verse skips the word say, so that God answers directly. This year, look at where it was placed, and at how it ends. Read in that spot, it speaks to the hungry person: you're not only holding back; you're close. A hadith in at-Tirmidhi names three people whose supplication is not turned away, and the first is the one fasting, until they break their fast. That's why the minutes before sunset fill with whispering. Now the ending. The verse goes on: so let them respond to Me, and believe in Me, so that they may be rightly guided. The word for God answering, ujib, and the word for people responding, yastajibu, come from the same root, j-w-b. In the verse, the answering runs both ways. God answers the caller; the caller is asked to answer back by trusting and acting. And the verse sets that two-way answer among the rules for the hungry days. Near, in the middle of the fast.
screen: `BETWEEN 185 AND 187` · `I AM NIGH. I ANSWER.` · `THE FASTING PERSON IS NOT TURNED AWAY` · `J-W-B: THE ANSWERING RUNS BOTH WAYS`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: whisper one du'a. If you pray, choose one thing you need, small or large, and say it quietly in your own words, the way people do in the minutes before sunset. You can begin by praising, as the Fatiha taught. If you don't pray, say one hope softly, so that only you hear it. Then sit in the quiet after it, and notice how close the quiet feels. The bell holds the time.
Close enough to answer. Al-Baqarah 2:186: I am near, I answer the caller, placed right in the middle of the verses on the fast. Today's word.
Your line: near, in the middle of the fast. Today, when you're hungry, tired or holding back from something, use that moment to whisper. Day three hundred fifty-two.

screen: `DAY 352 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DON'T EAT EACH OTHER'S WEALTH.`

353.title: Don't eat each other's wealth
353.hook: don't consume one another's property unjustly (2:188)
353.howItsDone: Islamic law forbids taking wealth by fraud, bribery, gambling or unjust contracts, and Muslims are taught to settle debts promptly; many cite 2:188 and the hadith of the piece of Fire when speaking of honest dealing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: close enough to answer, and your line, near, in the middle of the fast. Did you whisper anything? The fasting verses end, and the very next line is about money. Day three hundred fifty-three.
screen: `NEAR, IN THE MIDDLE OF THE FAST.`

segments.voice: All day in Ramadan, a fasting person doesn't touch food that is completely theirs. Their own bread, their own water, in their own kitchen, and still they wait for sunset. Now turn the page. The verse right after the fasting passage isn't about food at all. It's about other people's money. Some readers see a lesson in the order: if you can hold back all day from what is yours, you can hold back from what isn't. Today: don't eat each other's wealth.
screen: `YOUR OWN BREAD, UNTOUCHED UNTIL SUNSET.` → `TURN THE PAGE.` → `NOW, OTHER PEOPLE'S MONEY.`

segments.voice: Verse one hundred eighty-eight says: do not consume one another's wealth among yourselves falsely, and don't take it to the judges, so that you may knowingly consume a portion of other people's wealth in sin. The verb is eat. Arabic, like English slang, talks about eating money: swallowing it, devouring it. And the word for falsely is bil-batil: by what is empty, vain, without real right. Cheating, theft, fraud, gambling, a contract with a trick in it: commentators put all of them under this word. Then the verse names one particular trap: going to court to make the wrong thing look legal. A bribe to a judge. A clever argument that wins what you know isn't yours. Bukhari and Muslim preserve a hadith that goes straight at this. Umm Salamah reported that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told people bringing him a dispute: I am only human. One of you may argue his case better than the other, and I judge by what I hear. If I rule for someone something that is his brother's right, let him not take it. I am only cutting him a piece of the Fire. Even the Prophet's verdict, the hadith says, doesn't make a wrong thing clean. The court can be fooled. The one taking it knows. The verse says knowingly. Clean hands begin with what you already know is someone else's: the borrowed book, the overcharge you noticed and kept, the small debt you hoped they'd forget.
screen: `AFTER THE FAST, ABOUT MONEY` · `BIL-BATIL: WITHOUT REAL RIGHT` · `I AM ONLY HUMAN` · `THE COURT CAN BE FOOLED; YOU KNOW`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pay a small debt. Sit, and look honestly at what you're holding that isn't fully yours. Ten dollars a friend covered at lunch. A tool you borrowed months ago. A payment you've been late on. Change you were given too much of and didn't mention. Find one. Picture returning it, today, with a simple sentence: I owe you this. Notice how that sits with you. The bell holds the time.
Don't eat each other's wealth. Al-Baqarah's line right after the fast: don't take what isn't yours by false means, and don't use a court to make it look clean. Today's word.
screen: `DON'T EAT EACH OTHER'S WEALTH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: clean hands. Today, return or pay back the one small thing you found. Day three hundred fifty-three.

the Prophet on his own verdicts

what it means: don't take wealth by any false means, and don't use the courts to launder it.

354.title: The Hajj verses
354.hook: the pilgrimage, the months, no quarreling, remember Allah at Arafat (2:196–203)
354.howItsDone: Muslims who are able perform the Hajj once in a lifetime in the month of Dhul-Hijjah; pilgrims enter a state of ihram, avoid quarreling and indecent speech, and spend the Day of Arafah standing in prayer on the plain of Arafat.

segments.voice: Yesterday: don't eat each other's wealth, and your line, clean hands. Did you return the small thing you owed? Today, al-Baqarah sets out on a journey. Day three hundred fifty-four.

A stadium letting out. A train station at rush hour. An airport the day before a holiday. Crowds like that test anyone's patience, and the Hajj is a crowd on another scale: pilgrims from far-off countries, in the heat, old and young, all trying to reach the same few places on the same days. Tempers can fray anywhere. In the middle of its laws for this journey, al-Baqarah sets a rule about tempers. Today: the Hajj verses.
screen: `A STADIUM LETTING OUT.` → `A CROWD ON ANOTHER SCALE, IN THE HEAT.` → `A RULE ABOUT TEMPERS.`

segments.voice: Verses one hundred ninety-six to two hundred three are a short handbook for the pilgrimage. Complete the Hajj and the 'umrah for God. The pilgrimage is in the well-known months. And then verse one hundred ninety-seven: whoever takes on the Hajj in them, let there be no indecent talk, no wrongdoing, and no quarreling on the Hajj. The word for quarreling is jidal: arguing, disputing, wrestling with words. It's named in a place where arguments come easily: over a spot in the tent, a push in the crowd, who was first in line. A hadith in Bukhari says that whoever performs the Hajj without indecency or wrongdoing returns as on the day their mother bore them. Then the verse turns practical. Take provisions for the journey. And then: the best provision is taqwa, the mindfulness you met on the first page of al-Baqarah. The next verse adds a practical detail: there is no sin in seeking the bounty of your Lord, which the commentators say means trading during the pilgrimage season. Ordinary life isn't banned. Quarreling is. Then the verses move to the heart of it: when you press on from Arafat, remember God at the sacred landmark. Arafat is a plain outside Mecca where pilgrims spend one day standing in prayer. A hadith in at-Tirmidhi says simply: the Hajj is Arafah. The day at the center of the journey is spent remembering, not winning arguments. No quarrel on the journey.
screen: `A SHORT HANDBOOK FOR THE PILGRIMAGE` · `NO INDECENCY, NO WRONG, NO QUARREL` · `THE BEST PROVISION IS TAQWA` · `THE HAJJ IS ARAFAH`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go a day without arguing. Sit, and think about where today's arguments are likely to come from: a family member, a colleague, a comment thread, traffic. Picture the moment it starts. Picture yourself letting the other person have the last word, not because they're right, but because you're on a journey and this isn't what you're carrying. Breathe through the picture until it feels possible. The bell holds the time.
The Hajj verses. Al-Baqarah's handbook for the pilgrimage: the months, no quarreling, the best provision is taqwa, and remembering God at Arafat. Today's word.
Your line: no quarrel on the journey. Today, when an argument starts, let the other person have the last word, once. Day three hundred fifty-four.

355.title: What they ask about
355.hook: they ask about wine and gambling, and about orphans, and each gets a plain answer (2:219–220)
355.howItsDone: Islamic law forbids alcohol and gambling, encourages charity from what one can spare, and treats care of orphans as a weighty duty; guardians may share household life with orphans as long as they act for the orphan's good.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Hajj verses, and your line: no quarrel on the journey. Did you let someone have the last word? Today, instead of arguments, questions. Day three hundred fifty-five.

Scroll through any community's question board and you learn who they are. A parents' group: is this rash normal? A new neighborhood: where do I put the recycling? The questions are small and real and a little anxious. Al-Baqarah has a question board too. Again and again, a verse begins: they ask you. And what people asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ tells you who they were, a young community trying to live well. Today: what they ask about.
screen: `A COMMUNITY'S QUESTION BOARD.` → `THEY ASK YOU.` → `WHO THEY WERE.`

segments.voice: Yas'alunaka: they ask you. In al-Baqarah alone, the phrase comes again and again. They ask about the new moons. About what to spend, and on whom. About fighting in the sacred month. And in verses two hundred nineteen and two hundred twenty, three questions in a row. They ask about wine and gambling. The answer, in Pickthall's words: in both is great sin and some benefit for people, but “the sin of them is greater than their usefulness.” An honest answer: it doesn't pretend there's no benefit; it weighs. They ask what they should spend. The answer is one word, al-'afw: the surplus, what you can spare beyond your needs. And then they ask about orphans. Here the commentators tell the story behind the question. Abu Dawud records, from Ibn Abbas, that verses warning sternly against consuming orphans' wealth had come down, and guardians got scared. They began cooking an orphan's food separately, and if any was left over, they'd keep it apart until it spoiled. Everyone was miserable, and the orphan ate stale food. So they asked. And the answer is plain: doing what is good for them is best. And if you share your life with them, they are your brothers. God knows the one who spoils from the one who sets right. In the report, fear had made the rule harder than it was, a little like the cow all over again. The answer cuts through to the point: not whether the rule was followed perfectly, but whether the orphan is better off. Good for them is best.
screen: `YAS'ALUNAKA: THEY ASK YOU` · `WINE AND GAMBLING: WEIGHED HONESTLY` · `WHAT TO SPEND: THE SURPLUS` · `ORPHANS: WHAT IS GOOD FOR THEM`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer a question plainly. Think of a question someone has been asking you, out loud or with their eyes: a child, a partner, a colleague. Maybe you've been giving a long, careful, defensive answer. Or none. Ask yourself what is actually good for them. Then find the plain answer, one or two sentences. Say it to yourself until it feels true and simple. The bell holds the time.
What they ask about. Al-Baqarah's questions from a young community, about wine and gambling, what to spend, and orphans, each given a plain answer. Today's word.
Your line: good for them is best. Today, when you're caring for someone, ask only one question: is this good for them? Day three hundred fifty-five.

356.title: The Throne verse
356.hook: the Living, the Sustainer, whose Throne extends over heavens and earth, who never tires of guarding them (2:255)
356.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite Ayat al-Kursi after each obligatory prayer, before sleep, and when leaving home, and children often learn it early as a verse of protection.

segments.voice: Yesterday: what they ask about, and your line, good for them is best. Did you ask whether something was good for someone in your care? Today, the verse many Muslims call the greatest. Day three hundred fifty-six.

Count what you're guarding right now. Your phone's battery. A child's fever, or a parent's appointments. The inbox. The rent. The plant on the windowsill you keep forgetting. Most of us guard a dozen things at once, and by evening we're tired from it, sometimes too tired to sleep. Last year you heard the story of Ayat al-Kursi and the names inside it. This year we read it the way al-Baqarah places it, line by line, and end on its last picture: guarding without tiring. Today: the Throne verse.
screen: `COUNT WHAT YOU'RE GUARDING.` → `TIRED BY EVENING.` → `GUARDING WITHOUT TIRING.`

segments.voice: Read the verse just before it first. Verse two hundred fifty-four warns of a day when there's no trading, no friendship and no intercession. Every human safety net, gone. Then verse two hundred fifty-five answers: here is who holds everything when those are gone. In Pickthall's words: “Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him.” Then it widens, step by step. Everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him. Who could intercede with Him, except by His permission? So the intercession that verse two fifty-four took away comes back, but only through Him. He knows what's before people and what's behind them, and they grasp nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. Then the picture that names the verse: “His throne includeth the heavens and the earth, and He is never weary of preserving them.” The Arabic for never weary is la ya'uduhu: it doesn't weigh on Him, doesn't bend Him under the load. The word is used for a branch sagging under weight. Everything you're guarding, and everything everyone is guarding, the whole sky and earth, doesn't make Him sag. And the last line: “He is the Sublime, the Tremendous.” Many Muslims recite this verse after each obligatory prayer and before sleep. Notice why the bedtime habit fits. You lie down still guarding: the phone, the child, the rent. The verse hands the watch to someone who doesn't sleep and doesn't tire, so you can. He never tires.
screen: `NO TRADE, NO FRIEND, NO INTERCESSOR` · `THE ALIVE, WHO NEVER SLEEPS` · `ONLY BY HIS PERMISSION` · `LA YA'UDUHU: IT DOESN'T WEIGH ON HIM`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recite it once, understanding each line. If you know it in Arabic, say it slowly, and after each sentence, pause and recall what it means. If you don't, read it in English, one sentence per breath: the Alive, the Eternal; no slumber, no sleep; everything belongs to Him; no one intercedes but by His leave; He knows before and behind; His throne includes heavens and earth; guarding them doesn't tire Him; the Sublime, the Tremendous. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
The Throne verse. Ayat al-Kursi, al-Baqarah 2:255: the Alive, who never sleeps, whose throne includes heavens and earth, and who never tires of guarding them. Today's word.
Your line: he never tires. Tonight, before sleep, name one thing you're tired of guarding, and set it down. Day three hundred fifty-six.

357.title: No compulsion
357.hook: there is no compulsion in religion; the right way is distinct from error (2:256)
357.howItsDone: Muslims widely cite 2:256 as a foundational principle that faith cannot be forced; classical and modern scholars have discussed its scope, and many read it as a general rule for how Muslims relate to people of other beliefs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Throne verse, and your line: he never tires. Did you set something down before sleep? Today, the verse that comes right after it, and the end of a week. Day three hundred fifty-seven.

You can make someone sit through a sermon. You can make them memorize a creed, stand in a row, say the words. What you can't do is make them mean it. Ask any parent who has tried to make a teenager love a book, a sport, or a grandmother's favorite song. Right after the Throne verse, the one about who holds the heavens and the earth, al-Baqarah says something about forcing. Today: no compulsion.
screen: `YOU CAN MAKE SOMEONE SAY THE WORDS.` → `YOU CAN'T MAKE THEM MEAN IT.` → `RIGHT AFTER THE THRONE VERSE.`

segments.voice: Verse two hundred fifty-six, in Pickthall's words: “There is no compulsion in religion. The right direction is henceforth distinct from error.” Two sentences, and the second explains the first. The Arabic words are rushd, right guidance, maturity, and ghayy, straying. Some commentators read the link this way: the truth has been made clear, as clear as the verse before it, so there's no need to force anyone. A person sees, or doesn't, and chooses. Abu Dawud preserves a report from Ibn Abbas about why the verse came down. Some women of Medina, before Islam, had vowed that if a child of theirs survived, they'd raise it among a Jewish tribe. Years later, when that tribe was leaving Medina, some of those children, now grown and Jewish, were among them. Their Muslim parents wanted to hold them back and make them Muslim. The verse answered: no compulsion. Let them go as they are. The verse ends with a picture: whoever turns from taghut, the Qur'an's word for whatever is wrongly worshipped, and believes in God, has grasped the firmest handhold, which will never break. A handhold is something you grab yourself. Nobody can grab it for you. Scholars have discussed how far the verse reaches, and some early jurists limited it, while others have read it as a broad principle that belief can't be forced. Look back at this week: the fast that holds back, nearness in the middle of it, clean hands, a journey without quarrels, plain answers, the one who never tires. Each one chosen, not forced. No compulsion.
